newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Anti-Taleban air, land assaults appear to fail.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban air, land assaults appear to fail.

text.p: Fresh land and air assaults on Afghanistan's Taleban appear to have failed to significantly dent the purist Islamic militia's positions in Kabul and on the front to the north, witnesses said on Monday.
Airport sources said warplanes belonging to a northern alliance battling to expel the Taleban from Kabul dropped three bombs inside the airport perimeter on Sunday night.
But they said the bombers, sent by Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, struck well away from the runway and warplanes sitting in taxi areas, and caused no damage.
On Monday morning, two MiG-21s and a Sukhoi fighter-bomber were being readied to return to the battlefront, and there were no signs they would be impeded.

It was the second night running that Dostum, allied with ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, had sent bombers in an apparent attempt to stop the Taleban from using Kabul airport to strengthen their front lines.
One bomber hit a city centre park on Saturday night, but injured no one.

The Taleban, who drove Masood from the capital a month ago, have been using Kabul airport to send warplanes to bomb the alliance front lines and their main headquarters in the town of Jabal os-Siraj, some 90 km (60 miles) to the north.
Warplanes from both sides were busy on Sunday in the battle for a group of hills that straggle across a plain 25-30 km (15-19 miles) north of Kabul.
A Masood spokesman said late on Sunday the latest alliance bid to break through the Taleban lines had failed.
"We captured the high points which were planned," Abdullah said of the attack on the De Sabz pass, 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul. "But the whole pass has not been secured."

Afghan watchers in Kabul say the alliance forces must punch through the hills to be able to push the Taleban back across the plain to the fringes of the Kabul valley and to break out of vulnerable positions on their side of the plain.
An alliance source admitted as much.
"We are exposed. It is a problem," the source told Reuter correspondent Chris Bird on the northern side of the front line.

"The alliance problem is that they're going to have to move forwards or backwards. They can't stay where they are for much longer or the Taleban are just going to sit back and pound them to pieces from long range," said one Afghan watcher with a military background.
"I expect they will try again. They have to break the stalemate," he said of the alliance.
The front line has been static for a week and the Taleban are clearly regaining confidence after being pushed back from Jabal os-Siraj by a counterattack Masood launched just over two weeks ago.
The Afghan watcher said one strong sign of that confidence was a direct Taleban attack last week on Dostum in the far northwestern province of Badghis.
The Taleban say they have captured Badghis, pushed on into neighbouring Faryab province and were heading for its capital of Maimana, whose loss would be a very serious blow to Dostum.
There has been no independent account of the fighting in the remote region and Masood's spokesman, Abdullah, said on Saturday that fighting was still going on in Badghis.
The heavy fighting and the night raids -- the first on Kabul in 17 years of civil war -- indicates that ceasefire talks brokered by Pakistan and the United Nations had failed.
